title: How to Write Title Tags | AMK Digital Agency
description: What a title tag does, where Google gets the title link it shows, and a simple method for writing clear, unique page titles.

article.summary: The title tag is often the first thing a searcher reads. Here is how Google uses it and how to write one that is clear, unique and worth clicking.
article.author: AMK Digital Agency
takeaways: Every page needs its own clear, descriptive <title>.
Google can show a different title link if yours is unclear, stuffed or repeated.
There is no fixed character limit; long titles are shortened to fit the screen, so put the key words first.

blocks.text: How to write title tags that get clicked

blocks.html: The title tag is the <title> element in a page's code. Browsers show it on the tab, and search engines often use it as the clickable headline in their results. A good title tells people what the page is about before they click.

blocks.text: Where Google gets the title it shows

blocks.html: Google calls the headline in its results a title link. It is generated automatically. The page's <title> element is one of its sources, but Google can also use the main visible title on the page, other headings, the og:title tag, and the text of links pointing to the page.

blocks.caption: Google builds the title link from several sources on and around the page.

blocks.html: Because the title link is generated, you cannot force a particular title. You can make your <title> the clearest option, which makes it the most likely one to be used.

blocks.caption: Good and weak title patterns
rows: Describe the page in plain words
Searchers need to know what they will find
Write a different title for every page
The same title on many pages
Repeated titles make pages hard to tell apart
Keyword stuffing reads badly and can be rewritten by Google
Long repeated boilerplate on every title
Boilerplate pushes the useful words out of view

blocks.text: How long should a title be?

blocks.html: Google has no fixed limit on the length of a <title> element. In results, a title link is shortened as needed, usually to fit the width of the device. In practice, a title that is too long loses its last words, so put the most important words at the start.

items.title: Name the topic
items.html: Start with the main subject of the page, in the words your visitors use.

items.title: Add what makes the page useful
items.html: A benefit, a format or a detail: "guide", "price list", "for beginners", a place name.

items.title: Add your brand if there is room
items.html: Usually at the end, separated by a short divider such as | or -.

items.title: Check it
items.html: Read it as a searcher would. Is it clear, specific and different from your other pages?

items: Every page has exactly one <title> element
No two important pages share the same title
The main topic appears near the start
The title matches what the page actually offers

blocks.html: Our free Meta Tag Analyser shows a page's title, its length, and a preview of how it can look in search results.

blocks.question: Does changing a title guarantee a new headline in Google?
blocks.answer: No. Google generates the title link and may choose other text from the page. A clear, accurate title makes it more likely that your own title is used.

blocks.question: Should the title and the H1 be the same?
blocks.answer: They do not have to be identical, but they should describe the same topic. Google may use the main heading as a source, so a heading that matches the page's purpose helps.
